events.text: The county rolls say a village of two hundred pays tax on eleven people. The other hundred and eighty-nine, according to the rolls, died of the same fever in the same week, nine years ago, and have been farming ever since.

choices.text: Write them all back to life, and collect

effects.log: The revenue rises. The village stops greeting you. Your superior reads the total twice, and nods once.

choices.text: Write them back slowly, a few each year

effects.log: It will take ten years, and by then it will be somebody else's problem. The village headman sends a very large radish.

events.text: Two brothers have come to your desk to fight over one field. Each has a deed. Both deeds are in the same hand, and that hand, you notice, is the previous registrar's.

choices.text: Divide the field and burn both deeds

effects.log: Neither brother thanks you. They do both pay the fee. On the way out they begin arguing about the ditch.

choices.text: Look up who else that hand wrote deeds for

effects.log: The list takes three nights and fills a book. You put the book where you can find it, and do not mention it to anyone yet.

events.text: The magistrate has asked you, in passing, how many households there are in the county. You know the true number, the number on the rolls and the number the prefecture was told. He has not said which one he means.

choices.text: Give him all three, on one sheet

effects.log: He reads it, folds it very small, and asks you to dinner. You have a feeling you have been promoted, or marked.

choices.text: Give him the one that keeps the peace

effects.log: He nods as if that was the number he had in mind. You go back to your desk and sharpen a brush that was already sharp.

events.text: Four magistrates report to you now, and all four reports on last year's flood agree exactly, down to a misspelling. Somebody is writing them all, and they would like you to think nothing happened.

choices.text: Ride out and see the dykes yourself

effects.log: There is mud on your robes for a month. Three of the dykes exist. You write one true report, and it is the only one the capital ever reads twice.

choices.text: Summon the four and let them explain the misspelling

effects.log: They arrive sweating, and the youngest blames the eldest within the hour. The next year's reports are all different, and all much more careful.

events.text: A prefecture has a jail, and yours has a man in it who has been awaiting trial for sixteen years. No one can find the charge. He has started a small garden in the yard.

choices.text: Let him go, and keep the garden

effects.log: He asks if he may come back to water it. You find that you have no regulation against this.

choices.text: Find the charge first

effects.log: The charge is under the leg of a table in the archive. It is his brother's name. You let him go, and you have the archive searched from top to bottom.

events.text: A sect has built a new gate on the road through your prefecture and is charging for it. The pact says they are not yours to touch. The farmers who pay the toll say they certainly are.

choices.text: Buy the road from them, with the prefecture's silver

effects.log: It costs a year of road money, and nobody fights. The sect elder bows to you as to a good customer.

choices.text: Send a very polite letter citing the pact

effects.log: The gate stays, and the toll halves. The scholars in the capital admire your letter, and copy out the second paragraph.

events.text: The Minister signs what you put in front of him, and takes the credit in the Hall. This morning you put in front of him a memorial he should not sign, by mistake. Nobody but you has noticed yet.

choices.text: Take it back, and say why

effects.log: He looks at you for some time. From then on he reads the first line of everything, which for him is a revolution.

choices.text: Let it go up, and be ready

effects.log: It goes up. It comes back with a question on it, and the Minister spends a bad month. Everyone starts bringing you their papers first.

events.text: The ministry has thirty clerks and work for twelve. You have been asked to make savings. Every one of the thirty is somebody's nephew, and you have the list of whose.

choices.text: Dismiss the eighteen with the weakest uncles

effects.log: It goes quietly, because you read the list carefully. You receive three invitations and one small, well-made threat.

choices.text: Give all thirty real work

effects.log: For a year the ministry does more than it ever has. The other ministries complain about it bitterly.

events.text: Both factions have written to you on the same day, in the same friendly words, to ask what the Minister is going to do about the salt. Only you know that he has not heard about the salt.

choices.text: Tell the Minister

effects.log: He thanks you warmly, and asks you what he thinks about it. You tell him. By evening it is his firmly held view.

choices.text: Answer both factions, carefully and differently

effects.log: Both are satisfied, for now. You keep a copy of each letter, side by side, in a drawer that locks.

events.text: The edict came down in the Son of Heaven's own rough words, and he has told you to make it fit to be read. One small change of a word would spare a province. Nobody living would ever know it was you.

choices.text: Change the word

effects.log: The province is spared, and thanks the throne. You keep the first draft in your sleeve for a year, and then you burn it.

choices.text: Write what he said, beautifully

effects.log: He reads it aloud and is pleased with himself. You go home and do not sleep very well, and the next edict is on your desk by dawn.

events.text: A princess, a eunuch and the Chancellor's secretary have each mentioned, in passing, how much they admire your handwriting. All three would very much like to know what the next edict will say.

choices.text: Tell them all the same harmless thing

effects.log: Each believes that they alone have been told. It is a very small lie and you will be feeding it for years.

choices.text: Say nothing, and say it the same to all three

effects.log: It becomes known that the Grand Secretary cannot be got at. This is a good thing to be known for, and a lonely one.

events.text: The Chancellor is old, and has begun asking you to read his memorials to him, because of his eyes. Yesterday he asked you to write one for him, and sign it. He says that you have his hand by now, and he is right.

choices.text: Do it, and keep faith with what he would say

effects.log: The memorial is everything he would have said, with one less mistake. He has it read to him, and laughs until he coughs.

choices.text: Refuse, gently, and send for his physician

effects.log: He is cross with you for a week. Then he sends a jar of very old wine and no message at all.

events.text: Thirty soldiers are yours, and one of them is stealing from the other twenty-nine. They have all worked out who. They are waiting to see whether you have.

choices.text: Make him pay it back at drill, in front of them

effects.log: He carries the platoon's stores for a month, and the rest carry nothing. By the end he is cured, and the others have started to tease him, which is how you know it is over.

choices.text: Take him aside and ask why

effects.log: His mother, a debt, the usual. You send your own pay home with his for a season. Nothing goes missing again, and he would now walk into a river for you.

events.text: You marched them twenty li in the rain because the order said so. At the end of it a rider arrives with a second order, saying the first was a mistake. Thirty faces turn to you.

choices.text: March them back singing

effects.log: You start the song yourself, badly. It is the worst singing in the imperial army, and it reaches the camp before you do.

choices.text: Camp here, and write to the quartermaster

effects.log: They sleep dry for once. Your letter is short and polite, and it is read aloud in the officers' tent, with some enjoyment.

events.text: The youngest of your platoon lied about his age. He is fifteen at most, and he has just been sick behind the wagons after his first real fight. He begs you not to send him home.

choices.text: Make him your runner, away from the line

effects.log: He runs everywhere and grumbles constantly. He is the first to reach you with every order for the next three years.

choices.text: Send him home with his pay

effects.log: He cries, and he goes. Years on a farmer you have never seen stops you on a road, and gives you a chicken, and will not say why.

events.text: The garrison's grain tally and the garrison's grain have not met in some time. The man who kept the books was your predecessor, who has been promoted, and who has sent you a friendly note.

choices.text: Report the shortfall up the line

effects.log: It takes a year and makes you an enemy with a better title. The next tally is right to the last sack.

choices.text: Buy it back quietly and say nothing

effects.log: The soldiers eat. Your predecessor sends a second friendly note, and this one has silver in it, and you send that back.

events.text: Six hundred soldiers in a town of two thousand. The town would like you gone, and it would also like you to keep buying its wine. A soldier and a butcher's son have fought over this, and over a girl.

choices.text: Hold a court in the market, both sides heard

effects.log: The town comes to watch and stays to argue. The soldier digs the butcher a new drain, and the wine does not go up in price.

choices.text: Confine the battalion to the walls for a month

effects.log: Six hundred soldiers hate you for a month, and drill as they never have. The town sends a cart of wine to the gate, as a question.

events.text: A mountain sect has sent a polite master to look over your walls. He says that it is curiosity. He has also, you notice, counted your archers without moving his eyes.

choices.text: Show him everything, and offer him tea

effects.log: He is amused. He leaves you a note on where the wall is weak, and he is right. You fix it, and you wonder who else he told.

choices.text: Hold a drill he can watch from the road

effects.log: Six hundred turn as one. He bows from the road, not very deeply. The pact holds for another year.

events.text: A province musters to your banner now, and its gentry have sent you their sons, in very good armour, to be officers. None of them have ever been hungry. The sergeants have asked you, respectfully, what you would like done.

choices.text: Put them in the ranks for a year, armour and all

effects.log: The gentry write furious letters for six months. Then three of the sons turn out to be real soldiers, and the letters change their tune.

choices.text: Give them a company of their own, and watch it

effects.log: The province is delighted. The company parades very well. You make sure that it stands somewhere that does not matter.

events.text: The banner itself was made by the women of the province, nine months' work in gold thread. It has just been shot through at a border skirmish, and the soldiers are looking at it, and at you.

choices.text: Carry it into the next fight, holes and all

effects.log: It flies in rags, and the province hears of it. The next nine months' work is offered and you refuse it. The holes are now the point.

choices.text: Have the women of the province mend it, and make a feast of it

effects.log: The mending takes a month and the feast takes a week. Half your soldiers come home engaged, and you do not lack for recruits.

events.text: The Commander on your left will not move unless the Commander on your right moves first, over a matter of seating at a dinner fourteen years ago. There is a campaign in the spring.

choices.text: Hold a second dinner, and seat them yourself

effects.log: You use a round table and sit on the floor yourself. They are so offended, together, that they agree on everything.

choices.text: Order both to move at the same drumbeat

effects.log: They obey, each pretending not to have noticed the other. It is not friendship, but it does turn out to be a flank.

events.text: Every General on the frontier reports to you now, and every one of them is sure that the others are getting more grain. They are all correct about somebody, and you are the one who signs for it.

choices.text: Publish the whole allotment, to all of them

effects.log: There is a terrible week, then a grudging one. The Generals stop writing to you about grain, and start writing about the enemy.

choices.text: Keep it in your own head, and share as needed

effects.log: Each of them owes you something and none of them knows how much. It works very well for as long as you are never wrong.

events.text: The court has sent a eunuch to inspect the frontier. He is a small polite man with a very small polite notebook. Your Generals have asked whether they should show him the real fortifications.

choices.text: Show him everything, the rot included

effects.log: He writes for a month. The capital is displeased, and then in the spring the money comes. He sends you a small polite note, and it says only: "As you intended."

choices.text: Show him the good wall, and a very good dinner

effects.log: He leaves pleased, and full. The notebook, you learn later, has a page on how many walls you did not show him.

events.text: The empire's old enemy has sent you a gift across the border: a fine horse, a fine letter and a fine offer of peace, addressed to you and not to the throne. Your own staff saw it arrive.

choices.text: Send it all straight on to the capital

effects.log: The horse goes to the Son of Heaven, who rides it badly. Nobody at court can make anything of you this year, though several of them try.

choices.text: Keep the horse, and answer with a better one

effects.log: The frontier loves it. The court hears of it within the month, and there is a new tone in its letters. You sleep with the horse saddled.
